title: Electromagnetic and Acoustic Fano Interference in Surface Acoustic Wave Resonators
authors: P. K. Rath, J. M. Kitzman, M. Mesbah, C. Undershute, J. Pollanen
abstract: Surface acoustic wave-based resonators are sensitive probes of condensed matter systems, as well as surface-selective sensors for chemistry and biology. Surface acoustic wave devices have also been integrated into hybrid quantum systems with qubit platforms for applications in quantum information processing and sensing. The sensitivity of piezoelectric surface wave-based resonators to investigate these various systems can be enhanced by optimizing the device architecture and electrical measurement techniques. Alternatively, tailoring the spectral symmetry, arising from interference effects, offers a promising route to further improve sensitivity. In this work, we demonstrate the simultaneous introduction of both electromagnetic and acoustic Fano interference to shape the spectral response of GHz-frequency surface acoustic wave resonators. By systematically modifying the acoustic reflectivity of the resonators, we are able to isolate and analyze each interference mechanism independently. The broad range of temperature operation, from ambient to cryogenic temperatures highlights the potential for both classical and quantum sensing applications.
summary: This paper investigates enhancing the sensitivity of SAW resonators by engineering their spectral response using Fano interference. The authors demonstrate the simultaneous control of both electromagnetic and acoustic Fano interference by modifying the resonator's acoustic confinement. This technique proves that spectral asymmetry can be tuned, offering a promising route for advanced classical and quantum sensing applications.
main_problem: The primary goal is to enhance the sensitivity of Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) resonators for sensing applications by engineering their spectral response.
main_result: The work successfully demonstrates the simultaneous introduction of both electromagnetic and acoustic Fano interference to shape the spectral response, confirming that Bragg mirror design acts as a tunable knob for spectral symmetry.
method: The researchers measured the transmission spectrum ($S_{21}$) of SAW resonators across varying temperatures and systematically modified the acoustic confinement using different Bragg mirror configurations.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a SAW resonator fabricated on Y-cut LiNbO3, operating at GHz frequencies. The analysis models the spectral response using the Fano lineshape function, which accounts for interference between resonant and continuum scattering pathways.
key_observables: Spectral line shape asymmetry, quantified by the Fano factor ($q$), resonance frequency ($f_0$), and the temperature dependence of these parameters.
important_parameters: Temperature (ambient to $\sim 1 	ext{ K}$), acoustic reflectivity (controlled by Bragg mirror pairs), and the Fano parameter $q$.
main_assumptions: The interference effects can be separated by systematically modifying the acoustic confinement, allowing independent analysis of electromagnetic and acoustic contributions.
figures_summary: Figures show schematics of the interference setup, measured transmission spectra ($S_{21}$) exhibiting asymmetric dips, and plots detailing the temperature dependence of the Fano factor $|q(T)|$ and the resonance frequency.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of using Fano interference to enhance SAW sensor sensitivity. It details the experimental setup using multiple devices with varying acoustic confinement. The core of the work involves fitting the measured spectral data to the Fano lineshape function to quantify the interplay between acoustic and electromagnetic interference, concluding with temperature-dependent analysis.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer spectral features via controlled interference mechanisms (Fano resonance) provides a powerful, non-traditional method for enhancing sensor sensitivity, which is relevant for developing high-precision quantum transducers or detectors.

The case when q equals 0 corresponds to the absence of Fano interference and results in a Lorentzian line shape (see Eq. 1). FIG. 3. (a) The spectral response of the SAW resonator (Device I) at different temperatures. The curves have been vertically shifted relative to each other for clarity. As the temperature decreases, the resonant acoustic modes shift to higher frequencies and the asymmetry of the overall line shape increases. (b) Dependence of the magnitude of the Fano parameter |q| versus temperature. With decreasing temperature, |q| increases, indicating an enhancement of the resonant acoustic pathway over the non-resonant electromagnetic background channel.

FIG. 4. Fano parameter as a function of temperature for the three SAW Devices (Devices I, II, and III) with vary- ing acoustic confinement. Device I, having 20 pairs of Bragg mirror elements, (red points) exhibits the highest value of |q| across the entire temperature range. As the surface acoustic wave confinement is reduced in the other devices (i.e.Device II with 10 pairs of mirror elements (green points), and Device III with no mirrors (blue points)) we observe a reduction in |q|, indicative of a systematic reduction of phononic interference effects with decreasing acoustic confinement.
